extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, trademark practitioners, and other persons who practice before the USPTO (patent agents, patent attorneys, trademark representatives) and stakeholders in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria used by the USPTO (ALJ and Director) to assess practitioner misconduct, jurisdiction, signature/representation rules, and sanctions in proceedings involving patent/trademark practice before the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO jurisdiction to regulate practice before the Office
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress vested the USPTO with plenary, statutory authority to promulgate regulations 'govern[ing] the recognition and conduct of agents, attorneys, or other persons representing applicants or other parties before the Office.' (35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(D)). The Director may suspend or exclude a person from practice before the Office if the person is 'shown to be incompetent or disreputable, or guilty of gross misconduct,' or if the person violates regulations established by the Office. (35 U.S.C. § 32).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State law does not override USPTO authority to regulate practice before the Office (Sperry v. Florida ex rel. Florida Bar). The Director has authority to promulgate regulations related to the conduct of members and to discipline practitioners; arguments that Trademark rules/TMEP cannot form the basis of discipline are rejected where conduct violates those authorities or otherwise reflects unfitness to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of USPTO disciplinary rules to registered patent agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Registered patent agents are subject to the disciplinary jurisdiction of the Office. (37 C.F.R. § 11.19(a)). Both the former USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility (37 C.F.R. § 10.20 et seq.) and the current Rules of Professional Conduct (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.101 et seq.) apply to practitioners depending on when the misconduct occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misconduct that occurred before May 3, 2013 may implicate the former Part 10 rules; misconduct after that date implicates the new rules. Both may be implicated when conduct spans both periods; the former rules remain applicable to pre-effective-date conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for suspension or exclusion from practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director may suspend or exclude a practitioner if the person is shown to be incompetent or disreputable, guilty of gross misconduct, or violates Office regulations. (35 U.S.C. § 32; 37 C.F.R. § 11.19).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determinations consider the practitioner's conduct in light of disciplinary rules and relevant precedent; sanctions are imposed after weighing factors under 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a) — Disreputable or gross misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: "A practitioner shall not engage in disreputable or gross misconduct." (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a)). The regulation does not strictly define the term but has been interpreted to include unprofessional conduct or conduct violative of ordinary standards of professional obligation and honor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples treated as disreputable conduct include affixing clients' electronic signatures without authorization, filing trademark documents prepared by unauthorized foreign attorneys, continuing to act after an Exclusion Order, or attempting to conceal misconduct. Precedent (e.g., In re Lane) and the TMEP/trademark rules inform what practices violate ordinary professional obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4) and 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c) — Dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not 'engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.' (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4); 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forgery or knowingly signing another person's signature is deceitful conduct. Falsely representing that a document bears an applicant's actual signature (even if the document's substance is accurate) is a misrepresentation. Concealment or non-disclosure may also amount to misrepresentation. Examples in the record: entering applicants' electronic signatures when not authorized; filing Change of Correspondence Address forms that left an email address linked to the practitioner in order to conceal continued activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1) — Failure to correct misrepresentations made to the Office
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners have an obligation to correct misrepresentations made to the Office. (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting documents with false signatures or otherwise misleading the Office without correcting those misrepresentations violates this obligation. Concealment of continued practice after exclusion can fall within this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.77(a) — Handling matters beyond competence
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must not handle matters the practitioner is not competent to handle. (37 C.F.R. § 10.77(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acting in roles (e.g., prosecuting trademark matters) for which the practitioner lacks the appropriate qualification (such as being an attorney when required) can constitute misconduct under this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.505 — Aiding others in the unauthorized practice of law
rubrics_metrics.description: Aiding others in the unauthorized practice of law is prohibited (37 C.F.R. § 11.505).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepting payment to file, review, or sign documents prepared by foreign attorneys not recognized to practice before the Office, or otherwise facilitating their unrecognized practice before the USPTO, can constitute aiding unauthorized practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5) and § 11.804(d) — Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not engage in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5); § 11.804(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions that undermine Office processes, conceal violations, or otherwise impair the integrity of proceedings may be found prejudicial to the administration of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature requirements for filings (37 C.F.R. § 2.193; TMEP § 611.01(b)-(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: All correspondence and filings with the Office that require a signature must bear either a handwritten signature personally signed by the person named as the signatory, or an 'electronic signature' that meets the requirements of 37 C.F.R. § 2.193(c), personally signed by the signatory. 'A person signing a document electronically must personally enter any combination of letters, numbers, spaces and/or punctuation marks in the signature block on the electronic submission.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Another person may not sign the name of a qualified practitioner or other authorized signatory. There is no circumstance permitting a person to sign the name of another person. Entering another person's electronic signature and filing the document is a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: TEAS signature methods and their requirements (TMEP § 611.01(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three acceptable TEAS signature methods: 'Direct' (signatory personally enters name between two forward slashes; default); 'E-sign-on' (email text form to second party for signature, returned via TEAS); and 'HSign-On' (handwritten pen-and-ink signature scanned as PDF/JPEG and attached).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a document is downloaded and later filed, TEAS requires the electronic signature to be entered again to ensure contemporaneous verification of facts. If the filer intended to avoid contemporaneous signatory entry they should have chosen E-sign or H-sign; using Direct requires the signatory's contemporaneous personal entry. None of the methods permit signing another person's name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may be an authorized signatory on a filing (TMEP §§ 611.02, 611.03(a), 611.06(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents must be personally signed by the applicant or registrant, someone with legal authority to bind the applicant, or a qualified practitioner. For a juristic applicant, a person with legal authority to bind a corporation is a corporate officer (e.g., President, Vice-President, Secretary, or Treasurer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A non-attorney who is not a corporate officer and who is not a qualified practitioner cannot sign on behalf of a juristic applicant as the authorized signatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity requirements for Powers of Attorney (TMEP § 605.01; 37 C.F.R. § 2.17(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Valid Powers of Attorney must designate by name at least one individual qualified practitioner and otherwise comply with TMEP/37 C.F.R. requirements for recognition as a representative in a trademark case. A power of attorney does not permit a non-attorney to perform services that require a lawyer where law requires an attorney.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documents titled 'Powers of Attorney' or 'Authorization' that do not comply with TMEP/37 C.F.R. § 2.17 are insufficient to authorize a non-attorney to sign or otherwise act as a representative in trademark matters. Courts have held that a non-attorney may not use a power of attorney to engage in the unauthorized practice of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic representative / correspondent roles and limits (37 C.F.R. § 3.61; TMEP §§ 608.01, 609.04, 610, 611.06(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'correspondent' may transmit and receive correspondence; a 'domestic representative' may receive service of process or notice of proceedings affecting an application or registration for a foreign applicant. Neither a correspondent nor a domestic representative is authorized to prosecute an application or represent a party in a proceeding before the USPTO unless the domestic representative is also a qualified practitioner or someone with legal authority to bind a juristic applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activities that go beyond forwarding correspondence — e.g., preparing or prosecuting applications, signing responses or amendments — exceed the role of domestic representative/correspondent and can constitute unauthorized practice before the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'practice of trademark matters' (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)(2); TMEP § 608.01)
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of trademark matters includes preparing a trademark application; prosecuting a trademark application including submitting an amendment, response, or other document; and signing amendments and responses to Office actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only a licensed attorney (or otherwise qualified practitioner recognized by the USPTO) is authorized to represent an applicant or registrant in trademark matters before the USPTO. Non-attorneys are limited to administrative support roles unless otherwise authorized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign attorneys' recognition and limits (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.1, 11.14(a)-(c); TMEP § 602.03)
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign attorneys are not generally recognized to practice before the Office in trademark matters. Only in limited circumstances may foreign agents or attorneys file for reciprocal recognition to represent parties in their country (37 C.F.R. § 11.14(c); TMEP § 602.03).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing documents prepared by foreign attorneys who are not recognized under the reciprocal-recognition provisions is misconduct. A practitioner who files such documents or enables unrecognized foreign practice may be disciplined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violations of Trademark rules/TMEP may constitute misconduct even if not explicitly in disciplinary rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Although violations of the trademark rules or the TMEP are not per se disciplinary-rule violations, misconduct not specifically identified within the trademark rules or TMEP may nonetheless constitute misconduct for purposes of discipline (e.g., In re Edington; In re Reynolds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The trademark rules and TMEP set forth proper practices and procedures and offer guidance as to appropriate conduct; failure to follow them, and conduct reflecting adversely on fitness to practice, can support disciplinary findings under the USPTO's disciplinary framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment or non-disclosure can amount to misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A misrepresentation includes not only written or spoken falsehoods but 'any other conduct that amounts to a false assertion.' Concealment or even non-disclosure may have the effect of a misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing one's name from public correspondence but leaving an email address that continues to facilitate practice, or otherwise concealing ongoing participation after exclusion, can be treated as misrepresentation and deceit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Exclusion Order and obligation to comply
rubrics_metrics.description: An Exclusion Order directing a practitioner not to act as domestic representative or correspondent in trademark matters is effective immediately and practitioners who receive and understand the Order must cease the prohibited activities (e.g., Commissioner for Trademarks Exclusion Order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuing to file trademark documents, listing contact information that enables continuing representation, or otherwise assisting trademark matters after receiving an Exclusion Order constitutes further misconduct and supports disciplinary penalty (e.g., exclusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural/appellate standards in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may appeal an ALJ's initial decision to the USPTO Director within thirty (30) days; the Director may conduct a de novo review of the factual record and may affirm, reverse, modify, or remand the matter (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.55(a), (f); 11.56(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions are determined after consideration of factors enumerated in 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b). The Director reviews the record (including admissions) and may affirm the ALJ's findings and sanctions when supported by ample evidence.
